opus-5.5.text:
I think MTP plays quite different roles at different stages, and it's easy to conflate them.

**In pre-training**, I see MTP mainly as a richer training signal. With plain next-token prediction, the model can get away with local, short-horizon pattern matching. Asking it to predict several tokens ahead pushes the representations to encode more about where the sequence is going: planning, structure, longer-range dependencies. It acts like a densification of supervision. You squeeze a bit more learning out of each token of data, and as high-quality data gets scarcer, that matters. The benefit isn't uniform, though. It tends to show up more clearly at larger scales and on structured domains like code and math. At small scales it can even hurt a little, because you're spending capacity on a harder auxiliary task the model can't yet afford.

There's also a design question about how much MTP should interfere with the main objective. If the extra prediction heads are too heavy, or the loss weight is too high, they compete with next-token prediction. So we usually treat MTP as auxiliary: modest loss weight, lightweight modules that keep the causal chain, and sometimes a reduced weight later in training so the main objective dominates as the model converges.

**In post-training**, the role changes. RL and alignment rely on the model's own sampled trajectories, and it isn't obvious that keeping the MTP loss helps there. Often you can drop it or freeze those modules. What carries over is the representation quality it built during pre-training, not the objective itself.

**At inference**, MTP becomes an engineering asset. The extra heads can serve as a built-in draft model for speculative decoding. You predict several tokens, verify them in one forward pass, and if acceptance rates are high you get a large speedup with no separate draft model to maintain. For serving a big model cheaply, that's very practical.

So I'd summarize it this way: in pre-training, MTP is about learning efficiency and better representations. In post-training, it mostly steps back. At inference, it turns into a speed tool. The interesting research question is how to design it so that one module serves both the first and the last roles well, because what makes a good auxiliary training signal and what makes a good draft predictor aren't necessarily the same thing.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training MTP provides a richer learning signal and builds better representations for planning and longer-range dependencies, communicating an intended improvement to the base model.

r002.rationale: The response connects MTP heads to faster inference, but says post-training often drops or freezes them. It does not state that additional MTP layers are trained during post-training to accelerate inference.

fable-5.1.text:
MTP, multi-token prediction, is interesting precisely because it does different jobs at different stages, and I think people often conflate them.

In pretraining, the main value is as an auxiliary training signal. When you ask the model to predict not just the next token but the one or two after it, you're forcing the hidden representation at each position to encode more about where the sequence is going, not just the immediate continuation. In our experience that densifies the learning signal, you get more gradient per token of data, and it tends to help on tasks that require some planning, like code and math, more than on plain fluency. The cost is small if you do it with a light extra module rather than full extra heads, and we found the gains hold up with scale, which was the thing we were most worried about going in. One subtlety is how you structure the extra prediction. If the extra heads are fully independent, you lose the causal chain between the predicted tokens. Keeping a sequential structure, where the prediction of token t+2 conditions on the representation used for t+1, matters for the quality of the signal.

In post-training the role shifts. The auxiliary loss becomes less about representation learning and more of a regularizer, and honestly during SFT and RL you can often just drop it or scale it down. The data is much smaller, and you don't want the objective pulling the model in directions that compete with the alignment target. We treat it as something to tune rather than something sacred.

Then at inference the same module becomes a speculative decoding draft. The MTP head proposes the next few tokens, the main model verifies them in one pass, and you get a real throughput improvement with no change to the output distribution. That's where the design decision in pretraining pays off twice. If the head was trained jointly with the backbone, its acceptance rate is much higher than a separately trained small draft model, because it's seen the same data and shares the representation.

So my short answer is that it's a training trick first, an optional regularizer in the middle, and an inference accelerator at the end, and the architecture choice you make at the start determines how much you get out of the last stage.

r001.rationale: The response says MTP during pretraining improves learning signals and helps some capabilities, but it does not state that this uses one MTP layer.

r002.rationale: It describes post-training MTP as an optional regularizer and inference acceleration as a benefit of the module, but does not say that training additional MTP layers during post-training is intended to accelerate inference.

astra-6.text:
I think we should distinguish its role in pretraining, post-training, and inference. In pretraining, multi-token prediction is an auxiliary learning objective: the model has to learn representations that are useful for predicting several future tokens, rather than only the next one. The question there is whether that additional supervision improves the main model enough to justify the extra training cost.

In post-training, the priority changes. You’re shaping the model’s behavior, so you need to consider whether the MTP objective supports that process or competes with it. If you want to use the prediction heads for inference, keeping them aligned with the post-trained model also matters.

At inference, MTP can serve as a way to propose multiple tokens for the main model to verify. Then you care about acceptance rate and actual latency savings. So I wouldn’t treat MTP as having one fixed purpose: its value as a training signal and its value for inference acceleration are related, but they need to be assessed separately.

r002.rationale: The response connects MTP at inference with proposing multiple tokens and latency savings, but does not state that additional MTP layers are trained during post-training for that purpose.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate its role into pretraining and post-training. During pretraining, multi-token prediction gives the model a richer learning signal: it has to anticipate several future tokens rather than just the next one. That can encourage it to learn representations that are useful over a longer horizon, although the benefit depends on how you balance that objective with next-token prediction.

During post-training, the question becomes how to preserve that capability while adapting the model to follow instructions. If you want to use the MTP heads for speculative decoding, they need to stay aligned with the model’s updated output distribution. Otherwise, their predictions may be rejected more often, and the speed benefit shrinks.

So I think of MTP as both a training objective and a way to support faster inference. At different stages, you put different weight on those two goals.
